title: Yaji with Grains of Selim
author: Abidemi Olayiwola
desc: The kuli-kuli-heaviest blend — a full hundred grams of it against only two tablespoons of ginger, with eight pieces of grain of selim ground in.
longDesc: This blend goes the other way from the gingery versions: a hundred grams of kuli kuli against just two tablespoons of ginger powder, which makes it nutty and savoury rather than sharp. Eight pieces of grain of selim are crushed in with the kuli kuli at the start — the same spice the Delta pepper soups call urheri and the Igbo call uda — and then garlic, onion, pepper and salt are blended in. It is the only one of the documented blends to put a whole aromatic pod through the grinder alongside the groundnut cake.
equipment: Food processor, mortar and pestle, or coffee grinder
steps: Crush the kuli kuli and the grain of selim together in a food processor, a mortar with pestle, or a coffee grinder.
Add the remaining ingredients and blend to mix.
Store in a dry airtight container.
chefTips: Crush the kuli kuli and grain of selim together first, before anything else goes in. The groundnut cake protects the pods from over-grinding and the two combine better.
A hundred grams of kuli kuli to two tablespoons of ginger is the nuttiest of the documented blends. If you find commercial yaji too sharp, this is the direction to go.
Grain of selim is the same spice as urheri in the Urhobo pepper soups (NGA078) and uda in Igbo cooking. One ingredient, three regional names.
Eight pieces. The other blend that uses it calls for ten strands, so the two are close.
A dry container, and keep it dry. This blend has more groundnut cake than the others and it will clump if it takes up moisture.
No cloves and no stock cube. For a blend with cloves, the only documented one is the author's own peanut-powder version, which she flags as a substitution rather than a traditional blend.
If you cannot get kuli kuli at all, the honest move is to say so rather than swap in peanut butter powder and call it yaji.
commonMistakes: Adding the grain of selim with the powders rather than crushing it with the kuli kuli.
Over-grinding until the kuli kuli releases its remaining oil.
Treating the peanut-powder variant as equivalent.
sources: Adapted from 'How To Make Suya Spice At Home', byline Abi Olayiwola, eatwellabi.com. Headnote as printed: 'Easy homemade suya spice; 2 ways - with kuli kuli or peanut powder'. Quantities exactly as printed for the kuli kuli version: 100 g Kuli kuli; 8 pieces Grain of selim; 2 tablespoons Ginger powder; 2 tablespoons Garlic powder; 2 tablespoons Onion powder; 1 tablespoon Ground pepper; 1 teaspoon Salt. Yield not given.

Method as printed: 'Crush the kuli kuli and grain of selim in a food processor, mortar with pestle, or a coffee grinder'; 'Add the remaining ingredients and blend to mix'; 'Store in a dry airtight container.'

NOTE ON NOMENCLATURE: 'grain of selim' here is the same spice All Nigerian Recipes calls 'African Negro Pepper' (Xylopia aethiopica) in its blend — the two sources use different names for it, and the counts differ, 8 pieces against 10 strands.

KULI KULI IS PROPORTIONALLY FAR HIGHER HERE than in either of the other two blends — 100 g against only 2 tablespoons of ginger, where 9jafoodie uses equal volumes and All Nigerian Recipes uses 110 g to 75 g. Three named sources, three spice philosophies, not averaged.

HER SECOND VERSION, FLAGGED AS HER OWN SUBSTITUTION and recorded here because of what it reveals: the author explicitly states she uses peanut butter powder as a deliberate substitute for kuli kuli for readers who cannot get the traditional ingredient. That version is 4 tablespoons peanut butter powder, 3 tablespoons paprika, 2 tablespoons ginger powder, 1 tablespoon each garlic powder, onion powder and ground pepper or pepper flakes, 1 teaspoon cloves and 1 teaspoon salt. It is NOT published as a recipe here because it is a declared non-traditional blend — but it is the ONLY one of the four blog blends that contains cloves at all, and it is the one its own author marks as a deviation. Given that the academic description of yaji treats clove as canonical, that is a striking pattern worth recording.

The academic reference is Erhirhie Earnest Oghenesuvwe, 'Chemical Composition and Biological Effects of Yaji: A Popular Nigerian Composite Suya Sauce', Trends in Applied Sciences Research, 2019, 14(4), 215–225, which names seven components including clove and black pepper and quantifies none of them.
storage: 6 months in a dry airtight container.
healthBenefits: Defatted groundnut cake is high in protein and low in fat.
Grains of Selim is traditionally used as a digestive.
Garlic and onion powder carry organosulfur compounds.
culturalNote: That the only documented yaji containing cloves is also the one its author marks as a substitution is a small puzzle in the record. The academic literature treats clove as one of yaji's seven canonical components; three of four published home blends leave it out entirely. Either the blogs have drifted from the vendors' blend or the paper is describing something the home cooks do not make.
